abstract: A Clifford algebra is built from a space of directions together with a rule for their lengths, and this trail is a primer on its structure. [[t]] Products of basis directions form a basis of the whole algebra, even when the length rule is degenerate. [[c:sheaf.blade-basis-degenerate-forms-included]] Sandwiching by directions carries out every length-preserving symmetry, each one coming from exactly two such products that differ by sign. [[c:primer.twisted-adjoint-action]] Every real Clifford algebra is a table of real, complex or quaternion numbers, or a pair of such tables, in a pattern that repeats every eight steps. [[c:transport.classification-real-clifford-algebras]] The trail ends by showing that the position in that pattern belongs to the geometry, not to the bare algebra. [[c:dark-matter.residue-soldered-invariant-not-algebraic-one]] These are the tools the other algebra trails rely on. [[t]]
introduction: The walk starts with the multiplication table, moves through symmetries and the special product of all directions to the classification, and ends with matrix enlargements and what the geometry adds to the bare algebra. [[t]]
i:clifford-structure: These results describe a Clifford algebra from the inside: its basis, its symmetries, its centre, and its place in a classification. [[t]]
conclusion: The structure of a real Clifford algebra is fixed by its numbers of positive and negative directions, in a pattern that repeats every eight steps. [[c:transport.classification-real-clifford-algebras]] Yet the position in that pattern lives in the geometry, since bare algebra isomorphisms can forget it. [[c:dark-matter.residue-soldered-invariant-not-algebraic-one]] This trail rests on no postulate: each step is proved here or cited from results proved elsewhere and from the classical literature. [[t]]
t:^>sheaf.blade-basis-degenerate-forms-i: A Clifford algebra multiplies directions, and the first thing to know is what a basis of it looks like. [[t]] The products of basis directions, called blades, form a basis of the algebra for any length rule, degenerate or not, and for any choice of basis directions, perpendicular or not. [[c:sheaf.blade-basis-degenerate-forms-included]] The multiplication table depends polynomially, and so smoothly, on the length rule. [[c:sheaf.blade-basis-degenerate-forms-included]]
t:sheaf.blade-basis-degenerate-forms-inc: With a basis in hand, the next question is how elements move past one another. [[t]] Two perpendicular directions anticommute, and so moving a direction past anything built from directions perpendicular to it flips the sign of that element's odd part, the products of an odd number of directions, and leaves its even part alone. [[c:primer.commutation-rule]]
t:primer.commutation-rule>primer.twisted: That sign rule is what makes reflections work. [[t]] Sandwiching by a single direction reflects in the mirror perpendicular to it, with a sign twist for products of an odd number of directions, and each length-preserving symmetry arises from exactly two such products, differing by sign. [[c:primer.twisted-adjoint-action]]
t:primer.twisted-adjoint-action>primer.s: One product of directions is special: the product of all the basis directions, called the pseudoscalar. [[c:primer.sign]] Its square is always plus one or minus one: plus one exactly when the number of positive directions minus the number of negative ones leaves remainder zero or one on division by four, and minus one otherwise. [[c:primer.sign]]
t:primer.sign>primer.centre: The pseudoscalar also decides which elements commute with everything, the centre of the algebra. [[c:primer.centre]] With an even number of dimensions only the ordinary numbers do; with an odd number the pseudoscalar does too, so the centre becomes two-dimensional. [[c:primer.centre]]
t:primer.centre>transport.classification: These pieces assemble into the classification. [[t]] Every real Clifford algebra is a matrix algebra, a square table with entries in the real numbers, the complex numbers or the quaternions, or a pair of such tables side by side, and which one appears depends only on the number of positive minus negative directions, in a pattern that repeats every eight steps. [[c:transport.classification-real-clifford-algebras]] The algebra splits into two identical pieces exactly when that difference leaves remainder one on division by four. [[c:transport.classification-real-clifford-algebras]]
t:transport.classification-real-clifford: In odd dimensions the split has a simple reason behind it. [[t]] If the pseudoscalar squares to plus one, the algebra falls apart into two identical copies of its even part; if it squares to minus one, it behaves like the imaginary unit and the algebra is its even part with complex coefficients allowed. [[c:odd-extensions.doubling-or-complexification]] The even part is always a Clifford algebra of one dimension fewer. [[c:odd-extensions.doubling-or-complexification]]
t:odd-extensions.doubling-or-complexific: Elements equal to their own square, called idempotents, act like projections, and they mark where division fails. [[t]] In a nondegenerate real Clifford algebra, two idempotents are related by an internal change of viewpoint exactly when they project onto subspaces of the same size, in each block when the algebra splits. [[c:transport.classification-idempotent-orbits]] The ones that no such change can move are exactly the ones that commute with everything. [[c:transport.classification-idempotent-orbits]]
t:transport.classification-idempotent-or: The classification describes algebras as matrices, so it helps to know what taking matrices does. [[t]] Replacing an algebra by square matrices with entries in it changes its size but keeps its centre and its simplicity; matrices of matrices are just larger matrices, and the operation distributes over a sum of algebras. [[c:tower.matrix-amplification-structural-properties]]
t:tower.matrix-amplification-structural-: Since matrix enlargement keeps so much fixed, a bare algebra can hide where it came from. [[t]] The position in the cycle of eight, the residue, is kept by every isomorphism that carries directions to directions, but not by bare algebra isomorphisms, under which some different residues coincide at equal dimension. [[c:dark-matter.residue-soldered-invariant-not-algebraic-one]] For example, the algebra of our world and that of one of the series' candidate dark towers are the same bare algebra, and what tells them apart is which elements count as directions, which the metric fixes. [[c:dark-matter.residue-soldered-invariant-not-algebraic-one]]
